boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Port Walthall Junction record (May 6-7, 1864) in the Bermuda Hundred Campaign [May 1864]. Swift Creek (VA050) follows on May 9; the frozen description's 33,000 for the Army of the James is army-wide context. Army-wide returns, the campaign-wide casualty return and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads only 'Divisions'; the frozen description gives Butler's army 33,000 strong on landing, and the live force field reads 39,000 for the Union and zero for the Confederates. Humphreys gives the Army of the James 1,329 officers and 30,543 enlisted men of infantry, 82 guns and Kautz's 97 officers and 2,804 men of cavalry present for duty, and says Beauregard's arriving brigades gave about 19,000 effective infantry. Hagood reports an aggregate of about 1,500 men engaged on May 7 against at least two brigades, and Bushrod Johnson at the junction with some 800 muskets.
claims.rationale: Army-wide returns, a reconstruction of Confederate reinforcements not yet arrived, and one brigade commander's engaged count for May 7 only; the scopes and dates differ. None is adopted as a matched opening strength; live zeros are not measured absence.

claims.value: Humphreys says Butler sent a brigade out to the railroad on May 6 and some force from his two corps on May 7, and that Hagood's troops had been halted at the junction by Pickett, still in command at Petersburg. Hagood says Graham commanded on May 6 and that on May 7 he reported to Bushrod Johnson, who ranked him; Johnson withdrew the force to Swift Creek that night. The frozen commanders are Major General Butler (US) and Brigadier General Hagood (CS); the live page matches.
claims.rationale: Direction attributed as the sources state; Johnson and Pickett are not listed commanders. No listed commander receives automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Union victory, and both descriptions say a Union division drove Hagood's and Johnson's brigades from the depot and cut the railroad on May 7. Humphreys says the May 6 brigade returned after meeting some force and that the May 7 force encountered the enemy without any important result either way. Hagood says the enemy withdrew from the field before dark on May 7 and that his force was withdrawn to Swift Creek that night.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. The summaries and the Confederate report characterize May 7 differently; not reconciled.

open_questions: Butler's reports for May 6-7, Smith's, Brooks's and Heckman's reports (Nos. 45, 50, 62), Graham's (No. 101) and Johnson's (Nos. 95-96) reports, Hagood's casualty return (garbled) and the compiled Union return (No. 2, garbled) remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC (the live NPS page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Humphreys' The Virginia Campaign of ’64 and ’65 (1883) is an interested history by the Army of the Potomac's chief of staff, in the same author family as the registered From Gettysburg to the Rapidan; for this campaign it summarizes Smith's, Gillmore's and Weitzel's reports and quotes Beauregard's reports and telegrams, so it is not independent of the Beauregard family. Butler's telegrams and Hagood's, Barton's and Beauregard's reports, printed in Official Records Series I, Volume XXXVI, Part 2, are separate families of interested commanders' accounts; the volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
